title: Ames: believe-into-God fiducia — general assent causes it; special remitted-assent is its effect
source_text: XLVII. Sed illam proculdubio postea quoque didicerat ex Guil. Amesio, qui eodem plane modo Philosophatur de fiducia illa, quae est, juxta ipsum, fidei actus primarius atque essentialis. Fides ista, inquit, qua credimus non tantum Deum aut Deo, sed in Deum, est vera ac propria fiducia; non qua hac voce notatur certa & absoluta persuasio de bono futuro, sed qua significat electionem & apprehensionem sufficientis ac idonei medii, ac in quo persuasio & exspectatio talis fundatur. Quo sensu dicuntur homines fiduciam habere in sapientia, potentia, amicis, & opibus suis. In Medulla Theologiae, lib. 1. cap. 3. num. 13. Et postea numero 15. addit, Credere igitur in Deum, est credendo adhaerere Deo, inniti Deo, acquiescere in Deo, tanquam in vita ac salute nostra omnisufficiente. Unde concludit assensum generalem quem Dei verbo adhibemus non esse fidem salvificam, quia potest esse sine ulla vita: assensum vero specialem, quo statuimus Deum esse Deum nostrum in Christo, non esse actum primum fidei, sed actum ex fide emanantem. Nulla enim, inquit, est major in te quam in alio certitudo hujus veritatis, nec verior ejus apprehensio, antequam te ad Deum fide singulariter applicaveris. In fine tamen capitis subjungit, assensum illum solidum, qui adhibetur promissionibus Evangelii, fidem & fiduciam dici, quia nomen illud quodammodo meretur, sive consideretur ut est assensus generalis, quo firmiter credit aliquis veras esse gratiae promissiones factas credentibus & resipiscentibus: seu consideretur, ut est assensus specialis, quo credit aliquis se divinae gratiae jam esse participem; idque qua est assensus generalis parit fidem proprie dictam Amesio, id est, fiduciam, qua aliquis Deo adhaeret, & ei innititur: quatenus vero est assensus specialis apprehendens gratiae jam factae possessionem actualem, ex jam dicta fiducia fluit & enascitur. Adeoque, ex illius mente, assensus generalis est causa fiduciae, in qua proprie dicta fides consistit, assensus vero specialis est illius fidei effectus. Uterque tamen assensus improprie potest appellari fides secundum illum tropum, quo causae nomen effectui, & effectui quandoque nomen causae tribuimus. Assensus autem, inquit, ille solidus Evangelii promissionibus adhibitus dicitur fides & fiducia; partim quia parit fidem qua est assensus generalis; partim quia fluit ex illa fiducia, qua est assensus specialis & solidus apprehendens gratiae jam factae possessionem actualem. Sic enim nititur fiducia cordis, tanquam medio, vel argumento, cujus vi sola, conclusio talis potest inferri. Docet etiam experientia, particularem istam certiorationem intellectus in quibusdam deesse ad tempus, qui tamen fidem veram in cordibus suis habent interim latentem.
pass_a_gloss: But that distinction he had without doubt afterward also learned from William Ames, who philosophizes in entirely the same way concerning that trust which is, according to him, the primary and essential act of faith. That faith, he says, by which we believe not only God or unto God, but into God, is true and proper trust; not that by which this word marks a sure and absolute persuasion of a future good, but that by which it signifies the choice and apprehension of a sufficient and fitting means, and that in which such persuasion and expectation is founded. In which sense men are said to have trust in their wisdom, power, friends, and riches. In the Marrow of Theology, book 1, chapter 3, number 13. And afterward at number 15 he adds: To believe into God, therefore, is by believing to adhere to God, to lean on God, to rest in God as our all-sufficient life and salvation. Whence he concludes that the general assent which we give to God's word is not saving faith, because it can be without any life: but the special assent by which we lay down that God is our God in Christ is not the first act of faith, but an act emanating from faith. For there is, he says, no greater certainty of this truth in you than in another, nor a truer apprehension of it, before you have singularly applied yourself to God by faith. Yet at the end of the chapter he subjoins that that solid assent which is given to the promises of the Gospel is called faith and trust, because it somehow deserves that name, whether it be considered as a general assent by which someone firmly believes the promises of grace made to believers and penitents to be true: or whether it be considered as a special assent by which someone believes himself already to be a partaker of divine grace; and insofar as it is a general assent it begets faith properly so called in Ames's sense, that is, the trust by which someone adheres to God and leans on Him: but insofar as it is a special assent apprehending the actual possession of grace already made, it flows and arises from the trust already spoken of. And so, on his mind, general assent is the cause of the trust in which faith properly so called consists, but special assent is the effect of that faith. Yet either assent can improperly be called faith according to that trope by which we attribute the name of the cause to the effect, and sometimes the name of the effect to the cause. But that solid assent given to the promises of the Gospel, he says, is called faith and trust; partly because as general assent it begets faith; partly because as special solid assent apprehending actual possession of grace already made it flows from that trust. For so it rests on the trust of the heart as a means or argument by whose force alone such a conclusion can be inferred. Experience also teaches that that particular assurance of the intellect is absent for a time in some who nevertheless meantime have true faith latent in their hearts.
pass_b_english: Ames: primary essential act = believe-into-God fiducia (choose/lean on the sufficient means).
Not bare persuasion of a future good.
General Word-assent ≠ saving faith (can be lifeless).
Special ‘God is my God in Christ’ flows from faith — not faith’s first act.
General assent → causes fiducia; special remitted-possession assent ← effect of fiducia.
Particular intellectual assurance can be absent while true faith lies latent.
